issues.legal_issue: A person who executes a deed purporting to convey property as their own does not make a false document merely because they lack title, unless the execution involves impersonation, a false claim of authority, alteration, or another method of making a false document.
material_facts: The complaint alleged that the seller had no title to the land but executed registered deeds describing the land as the seller’s own.
The complaint did not allege that the seller impersonated the owner or claimed authority to execute the deeds for another person, or that the deeds were altered or obtained by deception.
The other accused were alleged to have participated as purchaser, witness, scribe, and stamp vendor.
issues.conclusion: The allegations did not disclose forgery, so the charges for forgery of a valuable security and use of a forged document were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 463 and 464 of the Penal Code require the making of a false document for forgery; section 467 applies to forgery of a valuable security, and section 471 requires fraudulent or dishonest use of a forged document with knowledge or reason to believe it is forged. A document is not made false merely because its maker dishonestly claims as their own property that belongs to someone else; the maker must fall within one of the statutory categories, such as falsely claiming to be another person or to act with another’s authority, altering a document, or procuring it through deception of a person unable to understand it.

predicates.criminal_charge_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging criminal charges or the refusal to discharge the accused.
predicates.seller_claimed_own_title: The seller executed a deed purporting to convey the property as the seller’s own.
predicates.seller_did_not_impersonate_or_claim_auth: The seller neither pretended to be the owner nor claimed authority to execute the deed on another person’s behalf.
predicates.document_was_not_altered_or_obtained_by_: The allegations did not describe an unauthorized material alteration or obtaining the document through deception of a person unable to understand it.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges charges based on a deed by which a seller claims property as their own, and the alleged execution involves neither impersonation nor false authority nor alteration or deceptive procurement, the forgery charges are not sustainable.

issues.legal_issue: A property transaction does not constitute cheating of a third-party complainant unless the accused deceived that person and thereby dishonestly induced the person to act, omit to act, or deliver or retain property in the legally relevant manner.
material_facts: The complainant alleged that the seller conveyed land that belonged to the complainant to a purchaser.
The purchaser was an accused, and the complainant was not the purchaser under the deeds.
The complaint did not allege that the accused deceived or induced the complainant to deliver property, consent to its retention, or do or omit anything.
issues.conclusion: The allegations did not disclose cheating, and the charge under section 420 was quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 415 and 420 of the Penal Code require deception and a resulting fraudulent or dishonest inducement; section 420 additionally requires the relevant inducement to result in delivery of property, consent to its retention, or the specified dealing with a valuable security. Alleging fraud or a false claim of ownership alone does not establish an offence unless the statutory elements of an offence are present. Sections 24 and 25 define acting dishonestly and fraudulently. The Court referred to Dr. Vimla v. Delhi Administration, AIR 1963 SC 1572, and State of U.P. v. Ranjit Singh, (1999) 2 SCC 617, on the meaning of defraud.

issues.legal_issue: A statement about obtaining possession under a deed does not constitute intentional insult unless it is made with intent to provoke a breach of the peace or another offence.
material_facts: When questioned about the deeds, the seller and purchaser allegedly said that they would obtain possession under the deeds and that the complainant could do whatever the complainant wanted.
The statement was described as referring to the consequences of executing the deeds; the complaint did not establish an intent to provoke a breach of the peace.
issues.conclusion: The allegations did not disclose intentional insult with intent to provoke a breach of the peace, and the charge under section 504 was quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 504 of the Penal Code requires an intentional insult made with intent to provoke a breach of the peace or the commission of another offence. A statement merely referring to the consequences of a property transaction does not, without that intent, satisfy the provision.

predicates.no_intent_to_provoke_breach_of_peace: The allegations did not show that the speaker intended to provoke a breach of the peace or another offence.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an intentional-insult charge based only on a statement describing transactional consequences, and the allegations do not show intent to provoke a breach of the peace, the charge is not sustainable.

issues.legal_issue: Charges for causing hurt and wrongful restraint should remain when the complaint allegations technically disclose those offences, even though the related property dispute does not support other criminal charges.
material_facts: The complaint alleged that the accused hit the complainant with fists and described conduct that the Court considered sufficient, at least technically, to show hurt and wrongful restraint.
The Court found that the allegations did not establish the separate offences of cheating, forgery, or intentional insult, but left the charges for hurt and wrongful restraint undisturbed.
issues.conclusion: The orders and charges for causing hurt and wrongful restraint were left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the complaint, taken as true, could technically disclose offences of causing hurt under section 323 and wrongful restraint under section 341 of the Penal Code. It also reiterated that a civil dispute may contain criminal ingredients and must be tried criminally when those ingredients are present, while criminal proceedings should not be used to pressure parties or settle civil disputes. The Court relied on G. Sagar Suri v. State of U.P., (2000) 2 SCC 636, and Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Ltd., (2006) 6 SCC 736.
